w5-root~idea.cta: What the root means on the Word road
w5-root~idea.title: What the root means
w5-root~idea.body: A root is the core of a word. "Dict" comes from Latin dicere, to say — so a dictionary is a book of sayings, and to predict is to say before.
w5-root~idea.more: I can say what a Latin or Greek root means.

w5-root~story.cta: What the root means on the Word road
w5-root~story.title: What the root means
w5-root~story.body: Inside many long English words is a short old word from Latin or Greek. Find it, and the long word opens up.
w5-root~story.more: Taught at: Word 5 · Latin and Greek roots — What the root means.

w5-find~idea.title: Find the root
w5-find~idea.body: Look for the root inside the word, and check the meaning fits: a portable thing can be carried. A word can contain the letters without the meaning — check both.
w5-find~idea.more: I can find the word that contains a root.

s5-caps~idea.cta: Capital letters on the Sentence road
s5-caps~idea.title: Capital letters
s5-caps~idea.body: A capital letter starts every sentence. Names of people, places, days, months and festivals get one too — and so does "I".
s5-caps~idea.more: I can put capital letters where they belong.

s5-caps~story.cta: Capital letters on the Sentence road
s5-caps~story.title: Capital letters
s5-caps~story.body: The capital letters have all fallen off this page. Quill needs help putting them back.
s5-caps~story.more: Taught at: Sentence 5 · Punctuation — Capital letters.

s5-caps~eg.cta: Capital letters on the Sentence road
s5-caps~eg.title: Capital letters: for example
s5-caps~eg.body: last monday priya and i… → Last Monday Priya and I…
s5-caps~eg.more: Taught at: Sentence 5 · Punctuation — Capital letters.

s5-end~idea.cta: How it ends on the Sentence road
s5-end~idea.title: How it ends
s5-end~idea.body: A statement ends with a full stop. A question ends with a question mark. A strong feeling or a "What a…!" ends with an exclamation mark.
s5-end~idea.more: I can choose a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark.

s5-end~story.cta: How it ends on the Sentence road
s5-end~story.title: How it ends
s5-end~story.body: Every sentence needs a full stop at the end — unless it is asking, or exclaiming.
s5-end~story.more: Taught at: Sentence 5 · Punctuation — How it ends.

s5-end~eg.cta: How it ends on the Sentence road
s5-end~eg.title: How it ends: for example
s5-end~eg.body: Where is my hat? · What a huge wave that was!
s5-end~eg.more: Taught at: Sentence 5 · Punctuation — How it ends.

s5-comma~idea.title: Commas
s5-comma~idea.body: Commas separate items in a list (eggs, milk and bread), follow an opening phrase (After lunch, we…), and mark who you are talking to (Mira, come here).
s5-comma~idea.more: I can put commas where they are needed.

s5-comma~story.title: Commas
s5-comma~story.body: Commas are tiny pauses that stop words bumping into each other.

s5-comma~eg.title: Commas: for example
s5-comma~eg.body: After lunch, we bought eggs, milk and bread.

s5-order~idea.cta: Build the sentence on the Sentence road
s5-order~idea.title: Build the sentence
s5-order~idea.body: English usually goes: who, does what, to what, then where or when. Start with the capital letter and end with the full stop.
s5-order~idea.more: I can put words in order to make a sentence.

s5-order~story.cta: Build the sentence on the Sentence road
s5-order~story.title: Build the sentence
s5-order~story.body: The words of a sentence have been tipped out of the box. Put them back in order.
s5-order~story.more: Taught at: Sentence 5 · Punctuation — Build the sentence.

s5-order~eg.cta: Build the sentence on the Sentence road
s5-order~eg.title: Build the sentence: for example
s5-order~eg.body: dog / the / barked → The dog barked.
s5-order~eg.more: Taught at: Sentence 5 · Punctuation — Build the sentence.

s5-apostrophe~idea.cta: Whose is it? The apostrophe on the Sentence road
s5-apostrophe~idea.title: Whose is it? The apostrophe
s5-apostrophe~idea.body: An apostrophe does two jobs. It shows belonging: the dog's bowl (one dog), the dogs' bowls (more than one dog), the children's coats. And it shows where letters are missing: can't = cannot, it's = it is. A plain plural never needs one: three apples. Watch "its": its tail means the tail belonging to it, with no apostrophe — "it's" always means "it is" or "it has".
s5-apostrophe~idea.more: I can use an apostrophe to show belonging or a missing letter, and leave it out of a plain plural.

s5-apostrophe~story.cta: Whose is it? The apostrophe on the Sentence road
s5-apostrophe~story.title: Whose is it? The apostrophe
s5-apostrophe~story.body: Quill the fox found a sign at the market: "Fresh apple's!" "Nothing belongs to the apples," laughs Quill, "and no letters are missing. That apostrophe has wandered in by mistake."
s5-apostrophe~story.more: Taught at: Sentence 5 · Punctuation — Whose is it? The apostrophe.

s5-apostrophe~eg.title: Whose is it? The apostrophe: for example
s5-apostrophe~eg.body: belonging: the dog's bowl · the dogs' bowls · missing letters: can't = cannot · it's = it is · plain plural: three apples (no apostrophe)
s5-apostrophe~eg.more: Taught at: Sentence 5 · Punctuation — Whose is it? The apostrophe.

s5-speech~idea.cta: Speech marks on the Sentence road
s5-speech~idea.title: Speech marks
s5-speech~idea.body: Speech marks go around the exact words someone says. The spoken words start with a capital letter. Their last mark — a comma, a question mark or an exclamation mark — goes INSIDE the closing speech mark, and the words that tell you who spoke come after. If the speaker comes first, put a comma after "said" and then open the speech marks. A new speaker starts a new paragraph.
s5-speech~idea.more: I can punctuate the words someone says.

s5-speech~story.cta: Speech marks on the Sentence road
s5-speech~story.title: Speech marks
s5-speech~story.body: Quill the fox is reading The Wonderful Wizard of Oz aloud and doing all the voices. "The speech marks tell me when to switch," says Quill, "and the commas tell me when to breathe."
s5-speech~story.more: Taught at: Sentence 5 · Punctuation — Speech marks.

s5-speech~eg.title: Speech marks: for example
s5-speech~eg.body: "Anyone would know that," said Dorothy. · "Are you a Munchkin?" asked Dorothy. · Bobbie said, "Come on, Phil; I'll race you to the gate."
s5-speech~eg.more: Taught at: Sentence 5 · Punctuation — Speech marks.

wr5-retell~idea.cta: Tell it back at the writing desk
wr5-retell~idea.title: Tell it back
wr5-retell~idea.body: A good retelling keeps the order: the beginning (who, where), the middle (what went wrong), the end (how it was solved). Use your own words — do not copy the book. Short is fine; clear is the point.
wr5-retell~idea.more: I can retell a story I heard, in my own words, in order.

wr5-retell~story.cta: Tell it back at the writing desk
wr5-retell~story.title: Tell it back
wr5-retell~story.body: You have heard a story in the Library. Now it is your turn to tell it — in your own words.
wr5-retell~story.more: Taught at: Writing 5 · Retelling — Tell it back.

wr5-retell~eg.cta: Tell it back at the writing desk
wr5-retell~eg.title: Tell it back: for example
wr5-retell~eg.body: Beginning: who and where. · Middle: the problem. · End: how it turned out.
wr5-retell~eg.more: Taught at: Writing 5 · Retelling — Tell it back.

sp5-show~idea.cta: Show and tell on the Stage
sp5-show~idea.title: Show and tell
sp5-show~idea.body: Hold it up. Say what it is. Tell where it came from, or a story about it. Say why it matters to you. Ask the room one question at the end.
sp5-show~idea.more: I can talk for a minute about something I chose, so others want to see it.

sp5-show~story.cta: Show and tell on the Stage
sp5-show~story.title: Show and tell
sp5-show~story.body: Everyone has a treasure: a shell, a medal, a book with a torn cover. Tell the room about yours.
sp5-show~story.more: Taught at: Speaking 5 · Show and tell — Show and tell.

sp5-show~eg.cta: Show and tell on the Stage
sp5-show~eg.title: Show and tell: for example
sp5-show~eg.body: What it is → where it came from → why it matters → a question.
sp5-show~eg.more: Taught at: Speaking 5 · Show and tell — Show and tell.

sp5-show~p0.cta: Show and tell on the Stage
sp5-show~p0.title: Something I would save from a fire

li5-simile~idea.cta: Like, as, or is? on the Literature road
li5-simile~idea.title: Like, as, or is?
li5-simile~idea.body: A simile compares two different things using "like", "as" or "as if": "I wandered lonely as a Cloud". A metaphor says one thing IS another, with no "like" or "as": "Hope is the thing with feathers". Both make us see something in a new way. The two things compared must really be different: hope is not a bird, which is what makes the metaphor surprising.
li5-simile~idea.more: I can find a simile and a metaphor.

li5-simile~story.cta: Like, as, or is? on the Literature road
li5-simile~story.title: Like, as, or is?
li5-simile~story.body: Quill said his tail was like a flame. Then he said, "My tail IS a flame." His friend looked worried and fetched a bucket of water. Words that compare can be very powerful.
li5-simile~story.more: Taught at: Literature 5 · Figurative language — Like, as, or is?

li5-sound~idea.cta: Voices and echoes on the Literature road
li5-sound~idea.title: Voices and echoes
li5-sound~idea.body: Personification gives a human action or feeling to something that is not human: "the brook laughing", "the waves beside them danced". Alliteration repeats the same first sound in words close together: "the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River". Personification is about MEANING; alliteration is about SOUND, so say the line aloud to hear it.
li5-sound~idea.more: I can find personification and alliteration.

li5-sound~story.cta: Voices and echoes on the Literature road
li5-sound~story.title: Voices and echoes
li5-sound~story.body: Quill was sure the brook was laughing at him. Then he noticed his own name in a line of poetry: "quick, quiet Quill". One trick gives things a human voice; the other makes words echo.
li5-sound~story.more: Taught at: Literature 5 · Figurative language — Voices and echoes.
